en: In the Jinacarita:
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Having paid homage with my head to the Great Sage, the most supreme;
The lotus feet of the Sugata, which bestow the honey of Nibbāna, are like bees to the virtuous;
they dispel the great darkness of delusion in the world, acting as a sun for the Dhamma,
manifesting with great splendor upon the mountain of the rising of the King of Dhamma.
The white water-lily of serene confidence, born from the lake of the hearts of living beings,
is ever awakened by the moonlight of the virtues of the Saṅgha and shines brilliantly with the rays of its stainless fame.
Therein, the beneficial life-story of the Conqueror is spread out extensively in every place.
Desiring to remember it always, I shall speak in brief:
for those who remember that sublime state, even the auspicious state is not difficult to attain;
if it is not difficult to attain, what need is there to mention the acquisition of worldly enjoyments?
Therefore, as I recite this sequence of words concerning the conduct of the mind—
beautiful, sweet, and pure, a nectar for the ears of the listener—
may you grasp it correctly and continuously with the cupped hands of your ears.
O virtuous ones, desiring neither old age nor death, partake [of this].
It is the abode for those seeking merit at all times, lasting for four hundred thousand aeons and beyond the countable.
Abounding in various jewels, crowded with diverse people,
filled with variegated market-stalls, and adorned with arches and flower garlands;
endowed with ten kinds of sounds, it resembled the city of the Lord of Devas.
The city known as Amarā became radiant and excellent.
Therein was born one of brahmin lineage, honored by the entire world,
possessed of great compassion and great wisdom, handsome and charming.
Named Sumedha, you were a prince who had reached the further shore of the ocean of the Vedas;
at the end of your life, you became a sprout of the Conquerors.
You were shown immeasurable wealth by the treasurer, the minister who increases the storehouse.
Beholding that vast accumulation of wealth gathered within hundreds of storehouses, he thought:
"Alas! My father and the others have gone to heaven without taking even a single māsaka coin with them."
"Overcome with spiritual urgency, Guṇākara addressed him:
'It is fitting for me to go now, taking Dhanasāra with me.
Having sat down in private in his own beautiful residence,"
Observing the defects in the body and even admonishing oneself, one reflects:
"The breaking up of this body is suffering, and its arising is also suffering;
I am subject to birth, subject to aging, and subject to disease."
Having thus seen many kinds of defects within the body,
he caused a drum to be beaten in the city and announced it to the king. When the time for supplicants had arrived,
accompanied by the sound of the drum and fragrant scents—
Then, for seven days, he was nourished by the flood of the essence of his giving.
But seeing that the grove of jewel-lotuses had not yet arrived—
despite the falling of even those frost-like drops of the gift— he was shaken.
While his circle of kinsmen wept,
that great hero emerged from his delightful home like a lordly elephant from a forest ablaze with fire, and he approached the vast Himalaya.
It was perfumed with the scents of yellow sandalwood, camphor, and agallochum;
and it was adorned with excellent *phalla*, *campaka*, *asoka*, and *pāṭalī* trees, as well as *tilaka*, *pūga*, *puṇṇāga*, *nāga*, and other such trees.
It was crowded with lions, tigers, and leopards, with elephants,
wild cats, and monkeys, and with various animals such as horses;
it was filled with mynas, cuckoos, and swans, with cranes, ospreys, and water-fowls.
It resounds with the warbling of birds such as pigeons and karavīkas,
and it is frequented by yakkhas, rakkhasas, gandhabbas, devas,
and dānavas, as well as by siddhas, vidyādharas, and other beings.
It was radiant with mountain ranges possessing the lovely luster of emeralds and sapphire-blue gems,
and with various mountains such as Mount Sājju and Mount Hemādri;
and it was brightened by numerous lakes and bathing-places with stairways made of gold and jewels.
It was resplendent there with many celestial maidens sporting about,
and it shone with hundreds of cascades covered in cool sprays of water,
and with delightful groves of kinnaras and uragas.
It was adorned with pavilions of creepers possessing the splendor of peacock crests, with courtyards covered in white sand,
and it was a treasury of many jewels such as gold, gems, and pearls.
For those people who desire [the world] and are attached to it,
he— the wise one— plunged into that abode which has merit for its pollen, situated within the thousand-eyed Sakka’s domain;
there, in that excellent leaf-hut, he saw the requisites of a seer.
Having assumed the guise of a householder and dwelling in meditative concentration,
that ascetic, within seven days, having produced the five higher knowledges as well as the eightfold attainments through the bliss of absorption, was rich in austerity.
One day, as the seer was traveling through the sky, he saw people clearing the highway.
Descending from the heavens there, he asked those people: "Why are you clearing the highway?"
"Sumedha, you do not know that the Tathāgata Dīpaṅkara,
having attained supreme enlightenment and set in motion the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma,
was performing the compilation of the Dhamma for the sake of the world."
Having reached the delightful city of Rammapura, he dwells here in Sudassana.
Together with four hundred thousand pure bhikkhus,
we invited him, the sole leader of the world, to accept our alms.
"O One with Vision, let us clear the path for his arrival," said the people to the ear, providing him with comfort.
Upon hearing the word "Buddha," their minds were set ablaze with rapture.
The mine of virtues was unable to remain steady in his own nature.
Therefore, the wise one, having quickly requested a small plot of ground,
obtained an uneven spot and began to level it.
In that very place, the Great Seer,
the benefactor of the world and the sole protector of the world, was worshipped by humans and gods alike, even though he did not adorn himself with ornaments.
He set out on the path together with his disciples.
Seeing the Tathāgata approaching, blazing with a mass of six-colored rays, he thought with great joy:
If I were to build a bridge for the steadfast Great Sage and his Saṅgha,
and lay down my own body in the mud, that would be for my long-lasting welfare and happiness.
Having reflected thus, the sprout of the Conqueror lay down.
Having awakened and beheld those beautiful lotus-eyes,
the steadfast one, still lying there, reflected once more in this way.
If I should desire to enter this excellent city today itself, having slain [my enemies] in the very next existence,
becoming a junior member of the Saṅgha—
what need have I for this disguise as a stranger, which only extinguishes my own afflictions?
"I am indeed a Buddha, having become a Buddha, the unsurpassed one in the world.
Having ferried the people across the ocean of existence with the boat of Dhamma,
and having brought them to the city of Nibbāna, my Parinibbāna is my supreme rest."
Having thought thus, he lay down there in the mud;
he shone like the trunk of a golden plantain tree.
Radiant with six-colored rays, he was resplendent.
Having seen the delightful physical form of the Sugata,
the wise one, his heart uplifted with born joy,
conceived a longing for supreme enlightenment.
Having come to that place, he saw the seer lying in the mud;
though he was a bridge for the world, he himself had become a bridge.
Standing at the head of that bridge to the world, he looked upon him.
The steadfast Tathāgata Dīpaṅkara, the Eye of the World, prophesied:
"In the future, this one named Gotama shall become a perfectly enlightened Buddha," and he likewise prophesied concerning his disciples and the city.
Having spoken thus and having performed that circumambulation together with the Saṅgha,
he who is dear to virtue honored [the Bodhi tree] with eight handfuls of flowers. Having done this,
he set forth together with the Saṅgha, like the Leader of the World himself.
Having heard the word of the Conqueror, the city named Rammaka— whose abode was filled with delightful gardens— rose up from the mire;
and, filled with joy, it was honored by hosts of deities with flowers and other offerings.
Having folded his legs crosswise, he sat upon a seat of flowers;
the one of great asceticism, great wisdom, and noble intelligence, whose senses were subdued.
The gods in ten thousand world-systems rejoiced.
They approached that wise one as he sat upon his flower-seat.
Seated there, he then contemplated the qualities that make a Buddha:
"What is above or below, or in the cardinal and intermediate directions?"
Investigating the entire element of phenomena (*dhammadhātu*) in this manner,
he first beheld the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*) within his own continuum.
Seeking further perfections in this very way, the wise one—
Having seen all the perfections with his own eye of wisdom,
he, wandering through saṃsāra, endured much suffering;
seeking the deathless, the noble one fulfilled the perfection of giving.
Like a wish-fulfilling tree for beings, like a wish-granting gem that bestows all desires;
he is the supreme among givers, bestowing whatever food and other things are desired.
O you with beautiful eyes, he has made the sky vast with stars.
The wise one, rejoicing, gave to supplicants after tearing it out—
his own body-flesh and even his blood— more than the dust of the earth and more than the water of the ocean.
Having adorned his head with a garland of flowers, he made it even higher than Mount Sineru;
shaking the earth, he gave away even his own sons as if they were mere objects.
Having fulfilled all the perfections, such as virtue, single-minded action, wisdom, and the rest—
Having passed away from that state as the husband of Vamā in his existence as Vessantara,
he was reborn in the beautiful Tusita city, the abode of the gods.
Having dwelt there for a very long time, he enjoyed unsurpassed prosperity.
Requested by the gods with palms joined, the Supreme among Bipeds said:
"O Great Hero, the time for your full enlightenment has come," and so forth.
Having thus observed the time and other factors, and knowing that it was the time for enlightenment, [he set out].
Having given his promise to the assembly of gods, he went to the Nandana grove.
Passing away from that happy destination among the hosts of gods,
the one of great wisdom, being extolled, fell from there and was reborn here.
Crowded with horses whose limbs and flanks were well-adorned,
abounding in the wealth of various wondrous goods in the markets,
and resplendent with lofty, delightful victory pillars.
Adorned with arches, banners, and flags, with decorated watchtowers and vast mansions,
it possessed well-guarded gates and most beautiful dwellings.
In the beautiful city of Kapilavatthu,
which brought joy even to Purindada,
he whose feet were served by the rows of jewels in the crowns of kings;

Depending upon King Suddhodana, the most excellent of rulers, the protector of the protectorless, the banner of the royal house of Okkāka, who is like a stainless lotus and the abode of manifold virtues.
With a pure and beautiful appearance, white as a garland of *sajjhu* flowers,
with a trunk grasping a white, excellent,
and beautiful lotus, he possessed the color of a noble elephant-king as white as the moon.
Having shown this through a dream, the one of vast wisdom [spoke] of her with lips like the bimba fruit,
eyes like blooming lotuses, and eyebrows that increased the beauty of the bow of the Lord of Gods.
To her whose excellent face is like the full, gentle, and stainless moon;
whose breasts are as beautiful as a pair of golden swans;
and who is lovely with lotus-feet and sprout-like hands.
He entered the womb of Queen Māyā, who was radiant with a golden-hued,
delicate complexion and adorned with the many ornaments of virtue, such as moral discipline.
At the moment of his rebirth-linking, many kinds of wonders arose for him;
then he was taken up with protection by both men and immortals,
upon the pericarp of a delightful red lotus.
Like a beautiful lioness statue made of emerald,
the golden-hued Lord of Bipeds reclined upon his couch within the mother’s womb.
Upon the mother’s mind-lotus, which was as clear as a gem threaded with a red thread,
the Wise One appeared, awakening it.
At the end of ten months, the Queen spoke this to the King:
"O King, I wish to go to my father's house. Then, having received the king’s permission,
they went to their own family home with great honor, possessing a splendor equal to that of the gods.
Having seen the grove of *sāla* trees adorned with clusters of fragrant flowers,
its lofty sounds being sung by swarms of bees,
as if calling out to the flocks of birds in its eyes—
Having found exceeding delight in that delightful Lumbinī grove, the abode of vast joy,
she— charming with the graceful movements and playful charms of an immortal maiden— remained there.
Having gone to the foot of a blossoming, excellent *sāla* tree,
he himself bent down a branch of the *sāla* and grasped it.
At that moment, the wind born of his karma [arose].
Having surrounded her with their cloaks,
the people stood still, guarding the queen; then,
having retreated from there, they remained well-composed.
With a hand adorned with clever and beautiful golden bracelets and other ornaments,
radiant with the rays of exceedingly copper-colored nails,
and exceedingly soft and beautifully red, [he] held a branch.
Standing right there, she bathed the steadfast one.
He shone with a delicate complexion like the color of gold,
possessing incomparable eyes that were delightful to behold, born from an incomparable womb.
Delightful with his pair of hands and feet gracefully extended,
like a golden swan entering a lotus pond;
[he was adorned] with a golden net that increased priceless joy, like Brahmā.
Taking it, they approached him and, having received it, stood before her and said: "Rejoice, O Queen! This son who has been heard by you as 'Aṅgīrasa' is now born."
Other men are born with limbs defiled by impurity,
but he was born as the most excellent lord of bipeds;
upon an exceedingly soft cloth of Benares silk, he was wrapped.
Pure like a beautiful gem set in gold that is even more priceless;
even so it was, yet two streams of water fell upon the body of that fortunate one as he stepped aside from the assembly.
They also caused a pleasant breeze to be brought for Janetti’s body for the sake of an auspicious rite;
their hands were like delightful antelope-skin mats.
Not taking it themselves, they approached and received [the hand] from him;
the gods, with a pillow made of fine linen, received the hand of the Hero,
that lion-king among men, for those foremost of men.
To them he was a bringer of joy, like the stainless moon;
with his broad feet marked by wheels,
he stood firmly established upon the surface of the earth facing the eastern direction.
Then, with their lotus-like wide eyes,
hundreds of women, along with men and gods,
gazed upon the single wheel-mark on his foot.
Honoring them with wise words and fragrant offerings, they spoke these words: "O wise one,
there is no one here equal to you."
"Where is there even one man more excellent than me?
Thus did the Lord of the World survey the world in every direction,
seeking even a single peer.
Facing north, he took seven steps and spoke these words:
"I am the foremost in the world, the eldest, the best," and so forth.
This was his supreme, unsurpassed proclamation, shared by no other.
Taking up that Lord of Men, who is worshipped by gods, asuras,
brahmins, and kings, the great multitude went to that well-adorned city called Kapilavatthu.
Though capable of bearing the weight of Mount Meru,
the king of mountains, and even all the waters of the ocean,
at the very moment of birth, she was unable to bear the burden of his virtues.
The earth seemed to tremble for that most excellent one.
The deer roamed with the dappled deer,
and the crows were exceedingly joyful with the owls.
The Supaṇṇa kings and the Mahoragas,
the hosts of cats and the mice,
and the deer met with the lions, the lords of beasts.
Just as parents [are drawn] by their children,
so too did the ship that had gone to a foreign land return to its own country,
having reached Kaṇḍa, the teacher Sarabhaṅga.
The great ocean there was adorned with various radiant lotuses,
its rows of waves ever tranquil,
and even the water itself [was pure].
It attained ultimate bliss.
The sky was filled with fully blossomed, hanging lotuses;
it ascended into the heavens.
The birds abandoned their flight in the sky,
and even the rivers stood still, no longer flowing,
due to the joyous union with the unseasonal clouds.
The Earth, most excellent of women,
was adorned as if by the gods themselves with many flowers rained down from the heavens, appearing exceedingly beautiful.
Delightful with ornaments of fully blossomed garlands,
her body embraced by a vine-like woman,
she is adorned with the finest garments of fragrant pollen.
The women from all directions made it exceedingly beautiful.
With fragrant incenses, the entire sky was perfumed and became most delightful.
The lords of the gods and asuras, assuming the guise of ascetics,
all wandered about accompanied by musical ensembles;
all people became speakers of pleasant words.
All directions were serene;
elephants trumpeted, lions roared,
and there was the neighing of horses.
In the sky, the flutes, lutes,
and divine drums each emitted their own beautiful melodies throughout the world-system as vast as the realm of the Lord of Mountains.
The radiance was sublime and delightful;
a pleasant fragrance arose with soft,
cool breezes that blew, bringing happiness to every living being.
May beings who are oppressed by manifold diseases be freed from them and become happy.
May they be fanned by the gentle breezes of the swaying tails of lions.
The world became delightful with light.
Breaking through the earth, the waters flowed;
people went to the Buddha with upright bodies.
The blind beheld the dances of the lame, graced with graceful movements;
the deaf heard the songs, so delightful to the mind;
and even the fire of Avīci attained a state of coolness for that time.
The water-born creatures rejoiced in it and laughed aloud.
For the hungry ghosts (petas) tormented by hunger and thirst, it became food;
even in the intermediate spaces between worlds, which were otherwise a continuous darkness, there was light.
The clusters of stars, the moon,
and the sun shone with even greater brilliance in the sky, as did the jewels upon the earth.
Breaking through the surface of the ground and emerging one above the other, they blazed forth.
Vast lotuses of five diverse colors blossomed beautifully;
and ornaments such as drums and the like, though neither struck nor played,
released an exceedingly sweet sound upon the earth.
Men who were bound with chains and other fetters were released from them;
the doors and bolts of the gates of the city spontaneously opened.
"Born in the city of Kapilavatthu, the son of Suddhodana..."
“Having sat upon the seat of enlightenment, he will become a Buddha.
Then, filled with joy, the hosts of gods in the abode of the Thirty-Three played, tossing their garments and performing other such acts.
The ascetic Kāladevala, possessed of psychic power and great wisdom,
was a frequent visitor to the family of the wise King Śuddhodana.
At the conclusion of his meal, he would go to the abode of the Tāvatiṃsa gods.
Having gone there to dwell for the day,
he sat in that palace and watched them playing while disguised as hunters;
he asked them the cause of their joy, but they did not tell him.
Having heard that from him, his mind burning with joy,
the Seer departed at once from that place and, having reached the residence of Suddhodana,
entered and sat upon a well-prepared seat.
“O Great King, it is said that an unsurpassed, pure son has been born to you.
We wish to see him,” he said. The king had the prince, adorned with ornaments, brought forward and approached him to pay homage.
Even for the Youthful One (Kumārabhūta), by the power of his virtues,
the delightful lotus-feet turned around and were placed upon the head of the ascetic.
By that very state of being, of him who is the supreme among men—
No one in the three worlds is to be venerated;
for if the head of the Lord of the Three Worlds were placed at the soles of the feet of an ascetic.
Raising his hands in the supreme *añjali* gesture, as if to pluck the blossoms from the tree of the ascetic’s excellence,
he stood before that wise one— an ocean of virtues— who had destroyed all unwholesome states.
Having witnessed that marvel of the God of Gods together with his own son, the lord of men—
Delighted, he paid homage at his lotus-feet, which were soft and marked with wonderful wheels.
When there was this great auspicious festival for the king, the city was adorned like the city of the gods;
those beautiful people, beautifully adorned, gathered at his supreme residence.
With his limbs adorned, preceded by those throngs of people,
the Lord of Men— having passed by that descendant of the Ikṣvāku line who was himself adorned with ornaments and who was an incomparable vessel of auspiciousness—
proceeded with the grace of the King of the Gods (Śakra) to the foot of a rose-apple tree, which was encircled by various beautiful and brightly colored creepers.
Having had him laid to rest outside, the groups of kinsmen went to behold that auspicious sight.
At the foot of the Jambu tree, radiant with its canopy shining like golden stars,
the Wise One sat upon a charming couch and, having made the opportunity, entered into meditative absorption.
Seeing him seated like a golden image, and his shadow standing as if fixed,
his kinsmen approached and said to him, "They say your son possesses such a wonder.
Having heard this from the lotus-eyed one, who was radiant like the pure moon in the sky, [the people were amazed].
Having said, "This is my second salutation," he bowed his head at his son’s feet.
Other various wonders born in the world have also been shown by me in brief,
for fear of excessive prolixity in this book.
In which [palaces] there were mansions adorned with various kinds of gems,
decorated with diverse canopies, couches, and seats,
and beautified by staircases, ladders, and many levels.
Adorned in a manner suited to the three seasons,
the clusters of rays from the celestial mansions constantly appear as if they were the very laughter of the sun upon their horns.
Like the morning sun over groves of lotuses,
they cause the lotus-thickets of the worlds to blossom.
They are always adorned with walls variegated with various gems.
Even without the reflection in a mirror, they adorn their own bodies.
There, the elixir for the eyes— resembling oil, a seat,
and a mountain— is seen, encircled by a rampart adorned with plaster.
In which moats there are always seen many lotuses, adorned with various jewels and encircled by bracelets of sapphire;
having reached great growth in that vast and charming place,
Having enjoyed sensual pleasures while dwelling there,
he, the sole eye of the three worlds,
went along the great road for a pleasure excursion in the park.
Having seen that form is worn out, diseased, and dead by means of time, one becomes dispassionate toward the three realms of existence;
and having seen the form of one who has gone forth, which is so enchanting—
Having taken his pleasure there during that fourth watch,

the one of great renown went to a delightful garden— a forest as beautiful as the Nandana grove, adorned with clusters of various trees in full bloom and resounding with the cries of flocks of peacocks and other birds.
In that delightful place, filled with the charming sounds of instrumental music, dance, and song, and possessing the splendor of the Lord of the Devas,
the Lord of Men, the Sovereign of Bipeds, enjoyed his desires at will. Then,
having folded his legs in the cross-legged posture, he sat upon his resplendent seat.
He thought to have his own body adorned.
Knowing his mind, Vissakamma, the lord of the gods, said this to him:
"Siddhattha, adorn yourself!"
Instructed by him, the illustrious Vissakamma went forth and wrapped his beautiful head with ten thousand pieces of cloth.
He also made his slender and charming body beautiful.
Resplendent with characteristics not shared by others,
he was adorned with various unsurpassed ornaments and with fragrant scents such as blue lotuses, sandalwood, and the like.
Adorned by that one whose limbs were adorned,
sitting there upon a stainless stone slab,
he was surrounded by women as beautiful as celestial nymphs.
Honored as if he were the Lord of Devas, he shone forth.
Having heard the supreme message sent by King Śuddhodana—
that "a son has been born to you, O son"— the Best of the Island-dwellers rejoiced.
Having said, "Today my bonds have been formed," he then went with all his desires to the beautiful city of Samiddha.
At that time, Kisāgotamī was standing on the upper terrace of the palace.
Seeing the king shining like the sun with its rays, you said this:
"Surely both the father of this wise man and his wife have attained Nibbāna,
for he possesses truly inexhaustible virtues."
Having heard such pleasing words spoken by her,
he went toward his own abode, swollen with joy that had arisen within him.
[He beheld] that necklace— cool, stainless, captivating, and increasing delight.
Having approached her and removed [the garment] from her neck,
he ascended the palace, as beautiful as the Vejayanta,
and lay down upon a magnificent couch like the King of the Devas.
Sundarī, resembling a celestial nymph, placed him at her head;
they performed dances and various songs as well.
Yet the wise one, delighted in renunciation, remained detached from the five sensual pleasures.
Even though such dances and songs were delightful, he took no pleasure in them.
Having lain down there upon his couch to rest for a short while,
the Great Hero, the lord of the earth, sat cross-legged.
Sitting there, having heard the various sounds of transformation from the young brides who had fallen asleep,
with a heart full of agitation, he thought, "I shall depart now."
Having gone to the delightful gateway of the city,
and having placed my head upon the beautiful rampart,
I shall listen there for the voice of the Wise One.
Having addressed his companion, the minister Acchannasavana— who was lying down, well-tamed, inspiring confidence,
and possessed of great merit— he spoke these words:
“Bring [the horse] named Kaṇṭhaka,” he commanded.
Channa, having received those words spoken by him,
went and quickly prepared the Sindhu-bred steed and brought it.
Knowing of his departure, that excellent steed, being prepared by him,
let out a neighing sound; that sound spread forth and reached the entire city.
All the hosts of gods did not hear anything from him.
Then, having seen his own supreme son first, Sajjanānanda said: "I shall become a Buddha after him."
Having thought thus, he went to his wife’s dwelling,
placed his feet upon the threshold, and thrust his neck inside.
It was strewn with flowers and resembled the couch of the Lord of Devas.
Beholding his own son lying on the bed together with his mother,
the Sole Leader of the World thought thus:
"If I were to remove the queen’s arm and [take] my own son..."
“We shall take her; she might even create an obstacle to my journey.
Having awakened with great affection, this Yasodharā [thought]:
“When I have become a Buddha, I will come back again and see my own child.”
Then the lord of men descended from that palace roof.
Yaśodharā, whose lotus-like face and hands were exquisite, radiant with the foam of her smile and the waves of her eyebrows,
and possessing blue-lotus eyes— like a moonlight night attended by a swarm of bees— that she was, [he beheld].
Who would be capable of abandoning such excellence of body, finding it standing supreme above all, without the Wise One?
"Master, I have brought the horse; know that the time has come, O Bull among Charioteers."
Thus spoke Channa to the illustrious protector of the earth.
Then the lord of the earth, having heard the words uttered by Channa,
descended from the palace and went into the presence of Kanthaka.
Delighting in the welfare of all beings, he spoke these words:
“O Kanthaka, do not carry me across this night, along with the world of men and gods.
Having become a supreme Buddha, I shall deliver the world.”
“[It is] from the ocean of existence, that mine of fierce crocodiles such as old age.
Having said this, he mounted the horse, which was white like a conch shell;
and having had Channa firmly grasp its tail, he [leaped].
Having reached the vicinity of the great gate,
he reflected: "If the gate were not opened by anyone at all,
then together with Channa, who has seized Kanthaka by the tail,"
"Having pressed down with my thighs this beautiful,
lofty wall, and having leaped over the rampart, I shall go"— thus thought the one of great strength.
Likewise, Channa, the supreme steed, was endowed with such firmness and power.
They considered each one of them as they crossed over the wall.
Having understood his mind, the gods stationed at the gate rejoiced in his auspicious journey and then opened the gate.
Thinking, "I shall turn this Siddhattha into Asiddhattha," he approached and, standing in the sky, spoke these words:
"O Great Hero, do not go forth from here; on the seventh day from now, [you must remain]."
“The divine Wheel-Treasure will surely appear!”—
when he was addressed thus by Death (Antaka), that one of great renown said to him,
“Who are you? and Māra identified himself.
“O Māra, know that I have attained the arising of the divine eye.
Go away from here, do not stay; I have no need for kingship.
Indeed, even the entire ten-thousandfold world system—”
“Having roared thus, I shall become a Buddha, the sole leader of the world.
When the Great Being had spoken these words,
that voice, unable to surpass his own speech, vanished right there.
Having spoken thus to the Evil One,
and having abandoned even the glory of a wheel-turning monarch like a morsel of food in the evening, I dwelt there.
Then, having gathered together to honor me as I was departing, they followed for some time.
Carrying thousands of jewel-lamps,
the Maruts went there behind him, in front of him, and on both his sides; likewise,

he then departed from the presence of the remaining lords of men like Indra departing from Mount Laṅkā;
trembling, he went with great speed into the presence of the Victor.
“O Bull of the Śākyas, this is not your lineage; do not wander, do not wander!
In this lineage, even the son of an unrighteous king did not formerly wander for alms.
When the Lord of Men had spoken thus, the Lord of Sages, the crest-jewel of virtues, [replied]:
“O Great King, this is your lineage, but mine is the lineage of the Buddhas,” he said,
as he revealed the lineage of the Perfectly Enlightened Ones to him;
and remaining right there, he further taught the sublime Dhamma.
Having spoken this most excellent, delightful verse beginning with “Arise and do not be negligent regarding the Dhamma,” which brings welfare to listeners,
the Supreme One granted them the supreme taste of the vision [of the Truth] and satisfied them.
Requested by him, he went to his dwelling together with twenty thousand such ones as himself;
having satisfied the Supreme among Men with sweet rice and drink, the lord of the earth [departed].
Having paid homage along with the king, whose hands were tawny with the rays of his crest-jewel,
she sat down in the presence of the Jina.
Those hundreds of beautiful royal ladies also went there.
Permitted by King Narinda, they then sat there.
Having taught the sweet Dhamma, the Conqueror, the ornament of the three worlds, said:
"Even I myself would not go today to the palace of Queen Bimbā."
"May my heart split from compassion for her"— thus he, the abode of compassion,
took his two foremost disciples and went to his father’s palace.
Having entered, the Buddha sat there upon the Buddha-throne.
The Bimba-lipped one, her body radiant with a mass of light resembling powdered emerald,
approached the presence of the Teacher like a trembling golden creeper,
shining as if she were the sun itself ablaze with a network of six-colored rays.
With the most excellent water, cool from contact with the Teacher’s feet,
he extinguished the great fire of sorrow burning in the fuel of his heart.
The King proclaimed to the Teacher the many virtues of Bimbā:
The Lord of Sages also proclaimed the Canda-Kinnara Jātaka.
At that time, when Prince Nanda had reached his three auspicious occasions—
namely, marriage, consecration, and entry into the household.
Even before the auspicious ceremonies had begun,
the Light-Maker (the Buddha) led him away to that most excellent and delightful monastery, as if against his will.
He brought his own son, who was following him for the sake of his inheritance, into the presence of the monks.
And also Prince Rāhula, resplendent with princely ornaments, uttered these dear words:
“May you be my pleasant shade,” and “Grant me my inheritance; grant me my inheritance.”
Having led him to the very monastery, he caused him to go forth into the unsurpassed state,
bestowing upon that wise one the inheritance of the jewel of the True Dhamma.
Having gone forth from there, Sumāli, the son of the Sugata, [tended] the lotuses of living beings in that place.
Causing [the world] to blossom with the rays of the true Dhamma, he has come once again to Rājagaha.
In the beautiful grove of trees thick with flowers, amidst clusters of lakes radiant with lotuses and water-lilies,
and in the Subha Sītavana where the white sands are adorned with many walking-paths, the Sugata dwells.
Then the preeminent merchant named Sudatta,
taking many goods on carts,
traveled from Sāvatthī to the delightful city of Rājagaha.
Having gone to the house of the merchant Sahāya,
he was addressed by that fortunate man: "The Buddha has appeared,
the Lord of bipeds in the world."
With a mind uplifted by joy that had arisen,
thinking "it is night" when it was actually dawn,
he went forth from there into the darkness-free light.
By the power of the gods, having traveled along the great highway,
he reached that most delightful Sītavana,
shining like the full moon.
Having seen that great seer, who was blazing like a lamp-tree and bringing joy to the eyes,
[he felt] supreme devotion for his feet.
Having received it with his head bowed,
the wise one listened to the profound, subtle, stainless, and excellent Dhamma;
and having attained the fruit of stream-entry, which is adorned with a thousandfold methods.
Having invited the Fully Enlightened One, the Leader of the World, together with the Saṅgha,
and having given a gift bringing happiness— endowed with beauty, fragrance, and flavor—
for the sake of the Teacher’s arrival at the excellent city of Sāvatthī.
Having received his promise, as he was traveling along the way,
at every yojana he gave and had constructed many magnificent monasteries, resplendent with artistic craftsmanship, spending vast amounts of wealth.
Returning again to Sāvatthī, which was adorned with hundreds of palaces and resplendent with arches,
stepped pediments, walls, gate-towers, and other structures,
it seemed at all times to mock even the city of the Lord of Devas.
"Endowed with every excellence and beautified by dance, song, and the like—
in what place might he dwell? Thus the Blessed One, the Leader of the World,
looked all around for a site suitable for a monastery.
The prince Jetarāja beheld a park resembling Nandana,
a stretch of ground endowed with shade, water, and other amenities;
he of great renown [surveyed it] as if by means of a carpet worth ten million pieces of gold.
Having purchased that preeminent [palace] there, which was enchanting to both men and gods,
ever beautiful with the sound of a network of tiny bells, crowded with golden finials like a horned beast,
delightful with a roof covered in many jewels, and adorned with strings of pearls;
He caused to be built a most excellent, vast, and variegated Gandhakuti, adorned with flowers and other offerings,
exceedingly radiant with canopies of diverse colors, a pinnacle of beauty;
and he also constructed a spacious dwelling for the offspring of the Conqueror.
Resplendent with various canopies, couches, and seats,
and beautifully adorned with rows of pavilions and the like,
it ever captivated the minds and eyes.
Moreover, there was a reservoir with soft, pure, white sand,
featuring a beautiful and spacious paved walkway,
its waters pleasant and exceedingly cool.
It was filled with fragrant and non-fragrant lotuses,
and it shone with fully blossomed *sāla*, *āsana*,
*soga*, *nāga*, *punnāga*, *pūga*, and other trees.
The merchant had the most excellent monastery named Jetavana built,
which was as enchanting as the highest peak of Mount Kelāsa.
Protected by the guardian deity Phaninda, who possesses a beautiful rampart,
that monastery— shining like a wish-fulfilling gem— accomplishes all the desired aims of the people.
Then Nāthapiṇḍika sent a messenger to the Lord of Sages for the purpose of his coming.
Having heard the messenger's message, the Teacher,
at that time, set out from there preceded by a great community of monks.
Having departed, he gradually reached the supreme city of Sāvatthī.
Taking up many beautiful, brilliantly shining banners,
the princes went before the Teacher like gods.
Then, following behind them, young women set forth,
just like celestial maidens carrying beautiful, full water-jars. Likewise,
the merchant’s wife took a full bowl and followed.
Together with many hundreds of lay followers, adorned with various ornaments,
the great merchant, accompanied by hundreds of other great merchants,
went forth toward the Leader, the Great Hero, having honored him in manifold ways.
Leading that excellent city to a golden hue with his delightful five-colored rays,
the Lord of Sages, the Sugata of beautiful limbs, [approached].
He sat down in the Jetavana monastery,
saying to the Teacher’s beautiful lotus-like hands: "I give this monastery to the Saṅgha of the four quarters,
with the Fully Enlightened One at its head."
Having sprinkled excellent, fragrant-scented water from golden jars,
he gave a delightful monastery, beautiful to behold.
He accepted that most excellent and well-constructed monastery.
Seated upon an invaluable and variegated throne,
the Lord of lords of men, the sole eye of the three worlds—
may that pleasing sight bring delight to the three worlds.
The Teacher [spoke] of the sublime benefit in the gift of a dwelling,
through that gift of a protector to him who was without a protector,
by the merchant named Sudatta.
Famous, seeking the welfare of others, and a great sage,
he was capable of describing the noble benefits of giving a dwelling—
even without the vast wisdom of the Buddha.
"O man, who is capable of praising the Lord of the Three Worlds even with many thousands of mouths?
Having thus spoken the Dhamma to him, he of vast renown—
Gladdening the minds of all people,
he dwells there, traveling from place to place, beating the great drum of the Dhamma with its most sweet sound.
Thus, the series of sites enjoyed by the Supreme One of the World, the Greatly Compassionate One who bestows benefit upon the three worlds— [sites] where gods,
asuras, mahoragas, rākṣasas, and others [constantly dwell]—
Now I shall demonstrate that which has been fully honored. The Victor,
like a garland of *sumana* flowers, causes the lotus groves of those to be trained to blossom with the masses of rays from the True Dharma.
The Supreme One made his dwelling for the first year in the Deer Park at the city of Bārāṇasī,
where there were rows of streets with shops filled with various kinds of jewels.
In the delightful city known as Pāṭaliputra,
the Lord dwelt during the second, third, and fourth rains retreats,
staying instead at the even more charming Veḷuvana monastery.
Relying upon the most delightful city named Vesālī, which shines with the rays from the crest-jewels of kings,
the Lion of the Śākya Munis dwelt on the fifth earth.
He made his dwelling in the great forest during the rainy season.
With eyes as beautiful as blooming, dark-blue, stainless lotuses,
he shone with the radiance of a body like refined gold.
The Buddha, the treasury of infinite virtues,
took up residence during the sixth year on the vast Maṅkula mountain.
His speech was sweet, profound, and more difficult for even the gods to perceive.
Having taught the Dhamma, the peerless one, the abode of glory,
the Sage spent the seventh rains-retreat on the cool and spacious stone seat of the Lord of Devas.
He whose feet are like full-blown lotuses, who dwells upon his own feet,
the conqueror of Māra, made his supreme dwelling on the eighth mountain named Suṃsumāragiri.
In the rainy season, amidst the terrifying forest thickets,
having destroyed the arrogance of the various heretical snakes— the many and diverse sectarians—
the ornament of the three worlds, in his ninth year;
The Victor, the king of birds, made his dwelling in the beautiful and most enchanting *simbali* grove of Kosambī;
he did so in order to pacify the great quarrel among those ascetics.
In the tenth year, the supreme sage,
worthy of the finest offerings, took up residence near that excellent elephant in a vast, stainless grove strewn with flowers.
Leading the people toward agelessness and immortality through the nectar of the Dhamma,
the Lord of Sages, whose teeth are pure and enchanting to the eye, dwelt at the excellent village of Nālā, known as Dijagāma.
The one of immeasurable wisdom made his dwelling for ten years in a monastery near the charming village of Verañjā,
which was delightful with fragrant flowers and fruits.
In his twelfth year, the All-Knowing Śākyamuni took up residence at the foot of the lordly *pucimanda* tree;
his face was like a blooming lotus, and he possessed the beautiful splendor of poetic art.
Out of compassion for the welfare of the world,
the Hero, the Honored One of the three realms, took up residence on Mount Ruciracāliya during his thirteenth year.
Delightful with hands and feet like bandhūka flowers,
the Lord of Dharma, the Wise One of great psychic power, dwelt in the most beautiful and excellent Jeta Grove during his fourteenth year.
Dedicated to the welfare of all beings, he made his dwelling there.
Having destroyed the rutting elephant of passion for kinsmen among those to be trained,
the lion-king of sages, in his fifteenth year of the rains retreat;
She made her dwelling in the jewel-cave of the delightful Nigrodha Monastery, upon the vast mountain of Kapilavatthu;
even a most harsh yakkha she brought to a state of perfect discipline.
Having led [the people] to the city named Varatamālavaka,
she took up residence there for ten and six months,
leading even a great multitude of people along the path of peace.
O Great Seer, in the excellent city of Rājagaha, which was delightful with its moats and adorned with walls,
gate-towers, dwellings, and archways, the Lord of Men took up residence during his seventh decade.
May the Dhamma— like a medicine that is sweet, brings happiness, and destroys the most terrible dust of passion for the world—
be desired throughout the three realms while it rains down.
During the rains, the Exalted One, the descendant of Aṅgīrasa, made his dwelling for ten and eight years on the most excellent Cāliya mountain.
He is the sublime enemy of the delusion of kinsmen and relatives.
Having slain [the defilements] with the sword of the Dhamma, the supreme King of Dhamma,
the Lord of the World, whose speech is sweet, again took up residence there in his nineteenth year.
With pure intention, he took up residence in the magnificent and variegated city of Rājagaha during his twentieth year;
he was a wish-fulfilling tree of beauty for the world’s pursuit of welfare.
The Lord of Sages, a wish-fulfilling gem and a most excellent auspicious jar,
thus honored by the three worlds and possessed of noble wisdom,
having made his dwelling unattached, wandered about after his first enlightenment.
The Blessed One, the sole kinsman of the world, whose variegated body was endowed with rays of six colors during the remainder of his time,
[dwelt] in Sāvatthī and in the delightful, preeminent Jeta’s Grove.
In the celestial abode and in the well-adorned Eastern Monastery,
the Sage dwelt for twenty-five years,
delighting in the welfare of the world and living in happiness.

Thus, for forty-five years, he who was immeasurably compassionate extinguished with the waters of the most sweet Dhamma the mass of fire of passion that had arisen in the forest of human beings and maidens.
May the cloud of the Sage’s teaching dwell [within us] and bring peace to the world!
May the noble lady of wisdom, born within the palace of my mind,
gladden all people and ever increase.
By the power of the merit gained from composing this account of the Conqueror’s life, I have reached the Tusita abode,
listening there to the teaching of the Dhamma from the World-Protector Metteyya.
Experiencing great glory for a long time together with him,
when the Buddha was born, that Great Being was conceived in the delightful city of Ketumatī within a royal lineage, endowed with the three causes for rebirth.
Having given robes, almsfood, and excellent, vast, and priceless lodgings and medicines to that Great Sage,
and having gone forth in his teaching, he illuminated that unsurpassed darkness.
Possessed of psychic power and mindfulness, correctly upholding the Three Pitakas,
he was prophesied by that Buddha as one who would become a Buddha in the future;
and having given gifts that bring happiness to each Buddha as they appeared, [he attained this state].
Wandering indeed through saṃsāra, he was like a wish-fulfilling tree for living beings,
giving whatever food and other things were desired, moving with sweet conduct,
and— being composed in mind— he gave his flesh, blood, eyes, and so forth.
Fulfilling all the perfections— virtue, renunciation, wisdom, and the rest—
and having reached the summit of the perfections, may you become an unsurpassed Buddha;
and having taught the sweet Dhamma that brings peace to living beings, may you bring about their welfare.
Having liberated the entire world, including the realm of the gods,
from the vast bonds of saṃsāra, may he reach the excellent, secure, and auspicious city.
By him who has become the ornament of Laṅkā and the banner of the lineage of kings—
Built by King Vijayabāhu under his own name,
it was adorned with a wall of stone and clay, gate-towers, and other structures; there,
dwelling in that delightful and excellent pariveṇa, he lived a life of peace.
This was composed by the wise Elder named Medhaṅkara,
an abode of compassion, who is always honored by the virtuous. In this work,
there are four hundred and seventy-three verses throughout its various sections.
In terms of the text, it consists of five hundred and fifty-five [verses].
